124.t: Bob Rolontz's label and Champion Jack Dupree's "Lonely Road Blues"
124.s: McRae recalls producing for Rolontz, taking Dupree to record "Lonely Road Blues" and Dupree's "When I Get Married".
124.q: trouble was, when we did this date with Mickey Baker and all those people -- the first time I did this date, everybody wanted to know who was the star. Because I had been doing recording dates. You know, I was writing for -- See, I was writing for a lot of dates, you know. And so when I went down…

124.t: How McRae became "Mr. Bear" and made "Walking the Blues"
124.s: At Glover's urging McRae worked with Jack Dupree, devising a record where he walked on a board while Dupree played blues.
124.q: When I was writing for King -- This is when I was telling about the years (inaudible) -- after we did -- before Bob Rolontz -- Glover had -- I had did the things for Wynonie Harris. And when Glover got over there he say, "Well" --

124.t: The flip side and the dubbed tape of "Walking the Blues"
124.s: McRae did a talking blues with Teacho Wiltshire for the other side and added rhythm by dubbing.
124.q: I say, "Do me a blues thing. Put it up tempo." And I told him (inaudible) started singing something to him (inaudible), you know.

124.t: Sid Nathan hears the dub in Cincinnati
124.s: Glover sent the tape to Sid Nathan, who loved it and planned to record it in Cincinnati.
124.q: I'm gonna go in the studio and get" -- see, Wynona (inaudible) in town -- some of the guys out there. He had a lot of musicians.

124.t: Release of "Walking the Blues" and Bob Rolontz's Groove label
124.s: King added a rhythm section to the tape and released it; RCA's new Groove label then invited McRae to record.
124.q: So he got that rhythm section out there. They stayed in the studio all day. Had a house band. They were just backing up different singers soming through, you know.

124.t: Making the Mr. Bear sides with an all-star band for Groove
124.s: Rolontz needed rhythm and blues artists; McRae gathered Mickey Baker and others, who were surprised he was the artist.
124.q: Yeah. Anyway, what we did, Bob Rolontz -- only he had Piano Red out of Chicago. See, he had a hard time getting artists because he didn't know too much about rhythm and blues. See, he took that job because RCA Victor wanted some of this rock and roll stuff. But they wanted to put it on RCA's label.…

124.t: Having Alan Freed's arranger sketch his dates; Mickey Baker's break
124.s: A rock-and-roll arranger sketched McRae's charts; guitarist Mickey Baker got a Groove date that produced the hit with Sylvia.
124.q: And they walked in and -- I think I got a guy who did all the writing for Alan Freed. What's his name -- I got him to do (inaudible), because he was doing all --

124.t: "Come On Honey" with McRae's tenor solo
124.s: They listen to a 1964 Enrica record and discuss the Sunsets' 1959 sides.
124.q: Yeah, this was one of the first ones--

380.t: Unissued RCA-Victor sextet sides, "Midnight With Sampson" and "Blues For J.T."
380.s: He goes through sextet titles with Marshall Royal and Chico Hamilton, a bossa nova "Perdido", and tunes dedicated to Bill Sampson and J.T. Gibson.
380.q: And here's another thing of my Sextet, with Marshall Royal, Maxwell Davis, Floyd Turner, Eddie Beal, and with Chico Hamilton on drums and Albert Calderone on timbales. This is one where I remember doing "Perdido" bossa-nova style, which was probably way ahead of its time. They didn't release that…

380.t: Filling in "details unknown" sessions: "Voodoo," "Poinciana" and "Dolphin Street Boogie"
380.s: He identifies sidemen on a label's dates and recalls fans asking him to sign an old 78 of "Voodoo" at a Sacramento festival.
380.q: Let's see. Including Maxwell Davis or Bumps Myers. Most of the time I had both of them on the date, on the same date. Their styles were very similar. But this was... I did some things for that company that I like very much. One was "Voodoo," which I know you never heard, but I happened to be up in…

602.t: Recording at J&M for Roy Brown: all-night party sessions
602.s: The Roy Brown sessions in New Orleans ran from evening to morning with drinks and sandwiches; Walter Daniels and Edgar Blanchett played.
602.q: Oh, yes. We used to have fun back then because I remember we recorded on Deluxe Records here, but we used to get a couple of bottles, you know, and we had more like fun, laugh and talk and just have drinks. We went in the studio one night.

167.s: Bunn describes Jules Bihari as a heavy-drinking man who started by catching acts and built the family record business, with Bunn helping him get into it.
167.q: He was a type. He was an alcoholic, boy. He was something else. As far as his clothes was concerned, he didn't care what you saw him in, to tell you the truth. He wouldn't press them and all, get them cleaned or nothing. I knew him. But he's been always nice to me. Anytime I call him and say,…

382.s: She once recorded an r&b version for a tape that may not have been released.
382.ch: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
382.q: I don't know. Somebody came up with the idea. I think it was at the same time, you know, when I got mad at these people who asked me to do a rhythm and blues. Somebody came up with this idea of doing this version of "Loch Lomond".
